# Results — Study 461 (Descending Triangle)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a
descending triangle (flat support + descending highs) breaks DOWN as drawn: short the support
break and ride the bearish continuation** — encoded as a mechanical rule. Pivots are confirmed
fractals (k = 5, with a 5-bar confirmation lag); over a rolling window of the latest confirmed
pivots we require descending swing highs and flat swing lows; a SHORT fires on the first close
below the flat support, entered at the **next close** (one documented lag), and we measure the
forward 5/10/20/60-day **short** return (so a textbook break-down shows POSITIVE). Offline &
deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **39** mechanical support breaks pooled across the 5 tapes (k = 5, lookback = 6) |
| Timing / costs | confirmed-fractal pivots usable only **+5 bars** later; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per break |

> **A rare pattern.** A mechanically-clean descending triangle (descending highs *and* a flat
> floor within tolerance) is uncommon: only **39 breaks** across five tapes over 21 years. The
> small sample is itself part of the story — the textbook figure that "appears everywhere" is
> mostly chart-reader pattern-completion, not a frequent mechanical event. Numbers below are
> honest but thin; we lean on the **direction** of the result and the synthetic control.

## The signal — support-break SHORT vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

The trade is a **short**, so a positive number = the break-down paid. One-sample *t* is against
zero; the **Welch short-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = short − random.

| horizon | n | short | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (short−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 39 | +6.2 bps | 46% | +0.15 | −58.1 bps | **+64.3 bps** | +4.2 bps | +1.58 | 0.119 |
| 10-day | 39 | −64.0 bps | 44% | −1.42 | −61.4 bps | **−2.6 bps** | −66.0 bps | −0.05 | 0.957 |
| 20-day | 39 | −152.7 bps | 28% | −3.40 | −64.9 bps | **−87.9 bps** | −154.7 bps | −1.43 | 0.158 |
| 60-day | 39 | −417.5 bps | 23% | −3.30 | −101.9 bps | **−315.6 bps** | −419.5 bps | **−2.57** | **0.012** |

Read it carefully. **The break-down does not resolve down.** Booked as a short, the rule *loses*
money at 10/20/60 days (−64 / −153 / −418 bps), with a 60-day win-rate of just **23%** — i.e.
after the "bearish" break, price went **UP** more than three times out of four. The only positive
number (+6.2 bps at 5 days) is a rounding-error blip that does not clear significance (Welch
*t* = +1.58, *p* = 0.12). And the short is *worse than a drift-matched random short* at every
horizon beyond 5 days; at 60 days the Welch *t* is **−2.57** (*p* = 0.012) — the support break is
**significantly worse** than shorting on random days. The negative one-sample *t*'s (−3.40, −3.30)
are partly the long-equity **drift headwind** every short inherits, but the *random* short eats
that same headwind and still loses far less. The descending triangle breaks the *wrong* way.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — the break-down loses almost everywhere

(Per-ticker counts are tiny — 3–21 breaks — so several HAC *t*'s are undefined; read the deltas.)

| ticker | breaks | short | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (short−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 3 | −215.7 bps | n/a | −60.1 bps | **−155.7 bps** |
| QQQ | 3 | −46.7 bps | n/a | −136.5 bps | **+89.8 bps** |
| IWM | 5 | −342.5 bps | n/a | −51.5 bps | **−291.0 bps** |
| DIA | 7 | −321.3 bps | −4.95 | −42.1 bps | **−279.1 bps** |
| GLD | 21 | −57.5 bps | −1.03 | −34.1 bps | **−23.4 bps** |

Only **QQQ** (3 breaks) shows a positive delta; in 4 of 5 names the short-the-break rule
*underperforms* a random short, and on an absolute basis the short loses in **all five**. No
coherent cross-sectional bearish edge — the opposite of what the folklore promises.

## Geometry placebo — scramble the descending highs, nothing changes

The decisive "does the *descending-highs* geometry matter?" test: keep the pivot positions, the
flat-support detection and the break logic, but permute which price sits at which swing **high**,
so the "highs descend" constraint becomes meaningless. If the descending ceiling is load-bearing,
the scramble should change the result.

| test | observed support-break 20d short | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY scrambled-highs triangle | −215.7 bps | **0.692** | 500 |

**69% of scrambled-geometry triangles match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.692). The
descending-highs constraint carries no information — geometric nonsense does just as well, so the
"triangle" is doing nothing beyond a generic (loss-making) support break.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real break-down

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* break-down continuation (knob `edge`), the same
support-break short behaves exactly as it must — so the flat/negative real-tape result is a
genuine "nothing there" (in fact "wrong way"), not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | short | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no continuation) | 13 | −31.7 bps | 38% | −0.43 |
| **0.50** (real planted break-down) | 8 | +1103.1 bps | 88% | +1.90 |

With no planted continuation the control sits near zero (*t* = −0.43, win 38% — no false
positive); a real planted break-down sends the short to **+1103 bps with an 88% win-rate** (the
small n caps the HAC *t* at +1.90, but the +35-point win-rate jump and the order-of-magnitude
return are unambiguous). The detector is live — it banks a genuine break-down when one exists.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The support-break short does **not** beat a drift-matched random short (Δ =
  +64 / −3 / −88 / −316 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the only horizon that is significant is 60 days,
  where it is significantly **worse**, Welch *t* = −2.57, *p* = 0.012). There is no usable
  short-side edge — booked as a short the rule loses at every horizon past 5 days.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Nothing to deploy: the short bleeds the long-equity drift headwind and
  then loses *extra* relative to a random short; costs only deepen the hole. The "measured-move
  target" never arrives because the break-down mostly reverses.
- **"Does the break resolve in the textbook direction?" — BUSTED.** It resolves the **opposite**
  way: the 60-day win-rate of the bearish short is **23%**, i.e. the "bearish" break is followed by
  a *rally* three times in four. And the scrambled-highs placebo (*p* = 0.692) shows the
  descending-highs geometry — the thing that makes it a *descending triangle* — is not load-bearing
  at all. The pattern is a description chartists draw after a pullback, not a forecast of breakdown.
